title: Krish's Learning Hub
checkin: Every Sunday at 7:48pm ET a check-in arrives in Claude. Reply with your repo link, your results table and your quiz answers from memory.
rules: A lab passes only when the output matches a reference, the README has real numbers from your RTX 4060, and you can answer that week's quiz without notes.
If a lab doesn't pass, next week starts by finishing it. No new material on a broken foundation.
The GPU track is the core. On heavy exam weeks, the two agent tracks can be dropped and made up later; the GPU lab cannot.
Stuck? Spend 20 minutes yourself, then ask in the GPU MODE Discord #beginner channel, then bring the error to Claude. Never sit stuck for more than an hour.

tracks.name: GPU Kernels
tracks.blurb: CUDA fundamentals for four weeks, then Triton, ending with a fused AV preprocessing kernel for NeuralDrive.
tracks.sessions: Mon lecture, Wed reading, Fri and Sun lab

tracks.name: Inference Systems
tracks.blurb: What Wafer works on: why LLM serving is slow, how vLLM and SGLang fix it, quantization, speculative decoding, and agents that write kernels.

tracks.name: Building Agents
tracks.blurb: Agent patterns, a tool-use loop from scratch, MCP, context engineering, evals and multi-agent orchestration. The capstone joins this track with Inference Systems.

modules.title: Setup and your first kernels
modules.goal: Write, launch and verify a 1D and a 2D CUDA kernel on your own 4060.

blocks.label: Mon: setup and lecture
items: Install with NVIDIA's [CUDA on WSL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/wsl-user-guide). Inside WSL install only the `cuda-toolkit` package, never `cuda` or `cuda-drivers`. Confirm with `nvidia-smi` and `nvcc --version`.

Watch the [freeCodeCamp CUDA course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=86FAWCzIe_4), chapters 2 and 3 (Setup, C/C++ Review). Clone the course code from [Infatoshi/cuda-course](https://github.com/Infatoshi/cuda-course).
Create the `gpu-kernels` repo with folders `01-cuda/`, `02-triton/`, `03-tensorrt/`, `04-jetson/`, `05-nki/`.

blocks.label: Wed: lecture and reading
items: Watch freeCodeCamp chapters 4 and 5 (Intro to GPUs, Writing Your First Kernels).
Read PMPP (4th ed.) chapters 2 and 3. No book yet? Watch GPU MODE Lecture 2 from the [lectures repo](https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures), which recaps those chapters.
On paper: draw 3 blocks of 4 threads and label which array index each thread handles.

blocks.label: Fri and Sun: Lab 1
items: `vector_add.cu` with a CPU reference, a `CUDA_CHECK()` macro and a bounds check. It prints `PASS`.
Time it with `cudaEvent_t` at block sizes 32, 128, 256 and 1024, with N = 10 million.
`grayscale.cu`: RGB to gray on a nuScenes camera frame using a 2D grid (`dim3`).
README with the block-size timing table and one sentence on what you noticed.

blocks.label: Practice: do at least 2
items: [GPU Puzzles](https://github.com/srush/GPU-Puzzles) 1 to 8 in Colab.
LeetGPU [Vector Addition](https://leetgpu.com/challenges/vector-addition).
One more beginner problem from [LeetGPU](https://leetgpu.com/challenges), such as Color Inversion.

quiz: Write the global index formula for a 1D launch and explain each term.
Why do you need `if (i < n)`? Give a concrete N and block size where it matters.
A kernel launch returns right away. What does that mean for timing, and what fixes it?
What is the grid size for N = 1,000,000 with 256 threads per block? Show the ceiling division.
In a 2D launch, how does a thread compute its (row, col), and how does that become an index into a row-major image?

modules.title: How the GPU actually runs your code
modules.goal: Explain warps, divergence, coalescing and memory-bound versus compute-bound, using your own measurements as evidence.

blocks.label: Mon: lecture
items: Watch GPU MODE Lecture 4, Intro to Compute and Memory Architecture ([lectures repo](https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures)).
Watch freeCodeCamp chapter 6 (CUDA API).

blocks.label: Wed: reading
items: Read PMPP chapter 4 and the coalescing section of chapter 6.
Read NVIDIA's [How to Access Global Memory Efficiently](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/how-access-global-memory-efficiently-cuda-c-kernels/).
Read Horace He's [Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles](https://horace.io/brrr_intro.html).
Look up your 4060's peak memory bandwidth (GB/s) and peak FP32 throughput (TFLOPS). Write them at the top of your notes.

blocks.label: Fri and Sun: Lab 2
items: `device_query.cu`: print SM count, max threads per block and shared memory per block.
`divergence.cu`: even/odd threads branching versus whole warps branching together. Time both.
`matmul_naive.cu`: one thread per output element, verified against a CPU matmul at 64×64.
Benchmark naive matmul at 512, 1024 and 2048. GFLOPS = 2·N³ / time. Record the % of your 4060's peak.
Optional: naive versus shared-memory transpose, following NVIDIA's [Efficient Matrix Transpose](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/efficient-matrix-transpose-cuda-cc/).

blocks.label: Practice: do at least 2
items: [GPU Puzzles](https://github.com/srush/GPU-Puzzles) 9 to 14.
LeetGPU Matrix Transpose.
LeetGPU [Matrix Multiplication](https://leetgpu.com/challenges/matrix-multiplication), naive version only.

quiz: What is a warp, and why should block sizes be multiples of 32?
What happens when threads in one warp take different branches? Use your divergence numbers.
Draw coalesced versus strided access for 4 threads. Why is one faster?
What is arithmetic intensity? Is naive matmul memory-bound or compute-bound, and how do you know?
Why do GPUs want many more threads than they have cores?

modules.title: Shared memory and tiled matmul
modules.goal: Have a tiled matmul you wrote yourself, benchmarked against naive and cuBLAS, and be able to explain why it is faster.

blocks.label: Mon: lecture
items: Watch freeCodeCamp chapter 7 (Faster Matrix Multiplication).
Watch GPU MODE Lecture 8, CUDA Performance Checklist ([lectures repo](https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures)).

blocks.label: Wed: reading
items: Read PMPP chapter 5 slowly. It is the tiled matmul chapter.
Read NVIDIA's [Using Shared Memory in CUDA C/C++](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/using-shared-memory-cuda-cc/).
On paper: trace one output element of a 4×4 matmul with 2×2 tiles through every tile phase. Mark each `__syncthreads()` and why it is there.

blocks.label: Fri and Sun: Lab 3
items: `matmul_tiled.cu` written from scratch, with the video and book closed.
Verify against your Week 2 naive kernel.
Try tile sizes 8, 16 and 32, and record GFLOPS for each.
Compare with cuBLAS `cublasSgemm`. It is column-major, so check your layout.
README table: naive vs tiled vs cuBLAS, GFLOPS and % of peak at N = 1024 and 2048.
Try the padding trick `tile[TILE][TILE + 1]` and note whether it changes anything.

blocks.label: Practice: do at least 1
items: The matmul puzzle at the end of [GPU Puzzles](https://github.com/srush/GPU-Puzzles).
LeetGPU [Matrix Multiplication](https://leetgpu.com/challenges/matrix-multiplication) again, now tiled. Compare with last week's runtime.

quiz: Why does tiling speed up matmul? Answer in terms of arithmetic intensity: how many times is each global value reused?
Where do the two `__syncthreads()` calls go, and what breaks if you remove each one?
What is a bank conflict, and how does the +1 padding avoid it?
Your tiled kernel versus cuBLAS: what is the gap, and what is one thing cuBLAS does that you don't?

modules.title: Reduction, profiling, and the CUDA midterm
modules.goal: Profile any kernel and say, with evidence, whether it is memory-bound or compute-bound.

blocks.label: Mon: lecture
items: Watch GPU MODE Lecture 9, Reductions.
Watch GPU MODE Lecture 16, Hands-on Profiling (both in the [lectures repo](https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures)).

blocks.label: Wed: reading
items: Read Mark Harris, [Optimizing Parallel Reduction in CUDA](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/1.1-Beta/x86_website/projects/reduction/doc/reduction.pdf).
Read PMPP chapter 10.
Skim the [Nsight Compute profiling guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html): memory throughput, SM throughput, occupancy.
Reward, only after your tiled kernel works: Simon Boehm's [How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel](https://siboehm.com/articles/22/CUDA-MMM).

blocks.label: Fri and Sun: Lab 4
items: Reduction v1 (interleaved), v2 (sequential), v3 (add during load), v4 (warp shuffle with `__shfl_down_sync`).
Measure each in GB/s and as a % of your 4060's peak bandwidth.
Run `ncu --set full` on naive matmul, tiled matmul and reduction v4.
For each, one sentence: memory- or compute-bound, plus the metric that shows it.
Top-level `01-cuda/README.md` with the matmul table, the reduction table and one Nsight screenshot.

blocks.label: Midterm: Sunday, no notes
items: Record a 5-minute screen recording (or explain at a whiteboard) covering: thread indexing in 1D and 2D, warps and divergence, coalescing with a drawing, why tiling helps, and one Nsight report walkthrough.

modules.title: Triton's programming model
modules.goal: Think in blocks instead of threads, and have a fused softmax that beats PyTorch's unfused version.

blocks.label: Mon: lecture
items: Watch freeCodeCamp chapter 8 (Triton).
Watch GPU MODE Lecture 14, Practitioner's Guide to Triton ([lectures repo](https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures)).

blocks.label: Wed: reading
items: Work through the [Triton tutorials](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/) Vector Addition and Fused Softmax, typing the code yourself.
Write a side-by-side note: what CUDA made you do by hand that Triton handles.

blocks.label: Fri and Sun: Lab 5
items: Triton vector add, benchmarked against PyTorch with `triton.testing.do_bench`.
Fused softmax: numerically stable, one row per program.
Benchmark it against `torch.softmax` and a naive multi-op PyTorch version across row widths.
Debug one kernel on purpose with `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`.
README with a GB/s table and one paragraph on why fusion wins.

blocks.label: Practice
items: Solve two problems you already did on [LeetGPU](https://leetgpu.com/challenges), this time in Triton.

quiz: CUDA programs one thread; Triton programs one what? What does `tl.program_id(0)` correspond to in CUDA?
What does the `mask` in `tl.load` do, and what CUDA line does it replace?
Why must `BLOCK_SIZE` be a `tl.constexpr`?
Why does fusing softmax save time? Count global memory reads and writes, fused versus unfused.

modules.title: Triton matmul, autotuning, and FlashAttention
modules.goal: Race a Triton matmul against your CUDA kernel and cuBLAS, and be able to teach online softmax.

blocks.label: Mon: lecture
items: Watch GPU MODE Lecture 12, Flash Attention ([lectures repo](https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures)).

blocks.label: Wed: reading
items: [Triton tutorials](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/): Matrix Multiplication, then Layer Normalization.
Read the [FlashAttention paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135), sections 1 to 3.
Read the Triton Fused Attention tutorial line by line and annotate it.

blocks.label: Fri and Sun: Lab 6
items: Triton matmul with `@triton.autotune`. Record which `num_warps` / `num_stages` config wins at each size.
Table: Triton vs your CUDA tiled vs cuBLAS at N = 1024, 2048 and 4096.
Run your BEV model with `torch.compile` and `TORCH_LOGS="output_code"`. Find one generated Triton kernel and explain what it fuses.
Write online softmax in plain Python and check it against `torch.softmax`.

quiz: Why is the N×N attention matrix a memory problem? Estimate its size for N = 8192 in FP16.
Explain online softmax: what two values do you carry between chunks, and how do you correct earlier partial sums?
What do `num_warps` and `num_stages` control?
Why does `tl.dot` with FP16 inputs run so much faster than FP32 on your 4060?

modules.title: Final project: a fused AV preprocessing kernel
modules.goal: NeuralDrive's camera preprocessing runs as one Triton kernel, with a benchmark you can put on your resume.

blocks.label: Lecture, any day
items: Watch GPU MODE Lecture 18, Fused Kernels ([lectures repo](https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures)).

blocks.label: Spec
items: Input: a `uint8` frame, HWC, BGR. Output: `float32` (with a `float16` option), CHW, RGB, normalized with per-channel mean and std. One kernel, one pass.

blocks.label: Deliverables
items: PyTorch baseline: flip channels, `permute(2,0,1)`, `.float()`, divide by 255, normalize.
Triton kernel, verified with `torch.allclose`.
Batch support for the 6 nuScenes cameras.
FP16 output option.
Benchmark grid: 640×480, 1280×720, 1920×1080 at batch 1, 4 and 6.
Achieved GB/s as a % of peak (it is memory-bound).
Plug it into NeuralDrive v2 and measure the end-to-end change.
Stretch: fuse the letterbox resize into the same kernel.

blocks.label: Final exam: Sunday, no notes
items: Record a walkthrough covering CUDA's thread model versus Triton's block model, why fusion helps memory-bound ops (with your numbers), online softmax, and your final project README.

modules.title: Anatomy of LLM inference
modules.goal: Measure prefill and decode separately on your own GPU, and explain why decode is memory-bound.

blocks.label: Tue: read
items: Read the [gpt-fast](https://github.com/meta-pytorch/gpt-fast) README, then `generate.py` start to finish. It is a complete inference engine in under 1,000 lines of PyTorch.
If you haven't yet, read the overhead and bandwidth sections of [Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr](https://horace.io/brrr_intro.html).

blocks.label: Tue: build
items: In `inference/week1/`, run a small instruct model (0.5B to 1.5B parameters fits in 8 GB) with Hugging Face `generate`.
Measure time-to-first-token (prefill) and tokens per second (decode) at prompt lengths 128, 1024 and 4096.
Write the KV cache size formula for your model (layers × 2 × heads × head_dim × bytes × tokens) and compute it at 4096 tokens.

quiz: What is the difference between prefill and decode, and which one is memory-bound?
What does the KV cache store, and why does it grow with sequence length?
Why does batching help decode throughput so much?

modules.title: Serving engines: PagedAttention and continuous batching
modules.goal: Serve the same model with vLLM and draw its throughput-versus-latency curve.

blocks.label: Tue: read
items: Read the [vLLM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180), sections 1 to 4. Focus on why naive KV allocation wastes memory and how paging fixes it.
Skim the [vLLM quickstart](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/getting_started/quickstart/).

blocks.label: Tue: build
items: Serve last week's model with vLLM in WSL.
Sweep concurrency at 1, 4, 16 and 64 requests. Record throughput (tokens/s) and p50 / p99 latency.
Compare tokens/s at concurrency 16 against your Hugging Face number from Week 1.

quiz: What is continuous batching, and how is it different from static batching?
What problem does PagedAttention solve? Use the words fragmentation and block table.
On your curve, where does adding more concurrency stop helping, and why?

modules.title: Quantization
modules.goal: Know what you trade when you quantize, with speed, memory and quality numbers from your own runs.

blocks.label: Tue: read
items: Read the [AWQ paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978), sections 1 to 3.
Look up which quantized formats vLLM supports on your GPU generation (Ada, sm_89).

blocks.label: Tue: build
items: Run the FP16 model and an int4 (AWQ or GPTQ) version of a slightly larger model in vLLM.
Record memory used, decode tokens/s and time-to-first-token for each.
Write 20 test prompts with expected answers and compare quality by hand. Note where the quantized model gets worse.

quiz: Why does weight-only int4 speed up decode but help prefill much less?
What does AWQ do differently from rounding every weight the same way?
When would you not quantize?

modules.title: Speculative decoding
modules.goal: Measure acceptance rate and real speedup from speculative decoding on your GPU.

blocks.label: Tue: read
items: Read [Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192), sections 1 to 3.
Read the speculative sampling section of [gpt-fast](https://github.com/meta-pytorch/gpt-fast).

blocks.label: Tue: build (light, midterm week)
items: Turn on speculative decoding in vLLM (n-gram or a small draft model).
Record acceptance rate and tokens/s on two prompt types: code (repetitive) and open-ended chat.

quiz: Why does speculative decoding produce exactly the same output distribution as the target model?
Why does it help more on code than on open-ended chat?

modules.title: Prefix caching and SGLang
modules.goal: Show a workload where prefix caching wins big, and explain RadixAttention.

blocks.label: Tue: read
items: Read the [SGLang paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104), sections 1 to 3. Focus on RadixAttention.

blocks.label: Tue: build
items: Build a workload where 50 requests share a 2,000-token system prompt and differ only at the end.
Run it with prefix caching off and on (vLLM or SGLang). Record time-to-first-token and throughput.
Write down which real products have this traffic shape (agents with long system prompts are one).

quiz: What does RadixAttention store in the radix tree, and when does it evict?
Why do agent workloads benefit so much from prefix caching?

modules.title: Agents that write kernels
modules.goal: Run KernelBench's evaluation on a kernel you wrote, and understand how agent-written kernels are scored.

blocks.label: Tue: read
items: Read the [KernelBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10517), sections 1 to 4, and skim the [KernelBench repo](https://github.com/ScalingIntelligence/KernelBench).
Optional: browse [Wafer Daily Kernel](https://docs.wafer.ai/daily-kernel) to see what a production version of this looks like.

blocks.label: Tue: build
items: Pick one Level 1 KernelBench problem. Write a Triton solution yourself.
Run the KernelBench correctness and speed check on it. Record the speedup over PyTorch eager.
Then ask Claude to write a solution to the same problem and run the same check. Compare: correct? faster? how many tries?

quiz: What does KernelBench's fast_p metric measure?
Name two ways an agent can cheat a kernel benchmark, and how a harness catches them.

modules.title: Capstone: a mini Wafer
modules.goal: An agent that searches serving configs for a traffic shape and ships the measured winner. Shared with the Building Agents capstone.

blocks.label: Deliverables (shared with Building Agents week 7)
items: Define two traffic shapes: short chat with high concurrency, and long-prefix agent requests.
The agent proposes vLLM configs (quantization, max batch size, prefix caching, speculative decoding), benchmarks each through your MCP tools, and keeps the winner per shape.
Every candidate must pass a correctness check before it can win.
README: the search log, the winning config per shape, and the speedup over default settings.

quiz: Why did the winning config differ between the two traffic shapes?

modules.title: Agent patterns, without a framework
modules.goal: Know the basic workflow patterns and build two of them with the raw Claude API.

blocks.label: Thu: read
items: Read Anthropic's [Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents). Make a one-line note for each pattern: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer.
Skim the Claude [tool use overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview).

blocks.label: Thu: build
items: In `agents/week1/`, build prompt chaining: a 3-step chain that turns a GPU lab README into a resume bullet, with a check between steps.
Build routing: classify a question as CUDA, Triton or other and send it to a different system prompt.
No frameworks this week. Just the API and plain Python.

quiz: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent, according to the post?
When would you choose orchestrator-workers over parallelization?

modules.title: The agent loop from scratch
modules.goal: A working tool-use agent loop of about 100 lines that you understand completely.

blocks.label: Thu: read
items: Read the Claude [tool use docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview) properly this time: tool definitions, `tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks, stop reasons.

blocks.label: Thu: build
items: Write an agent loop with two tools: `run_shell` (sandboxed to one folder) and `read_file`.
Add a max-steps limit, a stop condition, and a log of every tool call.
Task to test it: "compile and run my vector_add.cu and tell me if it passes."

quiz: Walk through one loop iteration: what goes to the model, what comes back, what you append.
Why does an agent need a max-steps limit even when the model is good?

modules.title: MCP: tools any agent can use
modules.goal: Your benchmark scripts exposed as an MCP server that Claude can call.

blocks.label: Thu: read
items: Follow the official [Build an MCP server](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/build-server) tutorial in Python.

blocks.label: Thu: build
items: Build an MCP server with `run_benchmark(script, args)` and `read_results(path)` tools for your `gpu-kernels` repo.
Connect it to Claude Desktop or Claude Code and have Claude run your Week 2 matmul benchmark through it.
These tools get reused in the capstone, so write clear tool descriptions.

quiz: What are MCP's three server capabilities, and which one did you use?
Why does the tool description matter so much to how well the agent uses it?

modules.title: Context engineering
modules.goal: Keep a long-running agent useful by controlling what is in its context.

blocks.label: Thu: read
items: Read Anthropic's [Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents).

blocks.label: Thu: build (light, midterm week)
items: Add a notes file to your Week 2 agent that it reads at the start and updates at the end.
Truncate large tool outputs to their head and tail, and log tokens per run before and after.

quiz: What is context rot, and what are two ways to fight it?
When is a notes file better than keeping the full history?

modules.title: Evals
modules.goal: An eval set for your agent, with a pass rate you can track as you change it.

blocks.label: Thu: read
items: Read Hamel Husain's [Your AI Product Needs Evals](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/).

blocks.label: Thu: build
items: Write 20 test tasks for your agent with checkable outcomes (a file exists, a benchmark ran, a number is in range).
Run all 20, record the pass rate, and read every failure. Group failures into 3 to 5 types.
Fix the most common failure type and rerun. Record the new pass rate.

quiz: What are the three levels of evals in the post?
Why look at every failure by hand before building automated graders?

modules.title: Multi-agent orchestration
modules.goal: An orchestrator that splits work across parallel workers and merges the results.

blocks.label: Thu: read
items: Read Anthropic's [How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system).

blocks.label: Thu: build
items: Build an orchestrator that gets a goal ("find the best block size for my matmul"), spawns 3 workers that each benchmark a different range in parallel, then merges their findings.
Log total tokens and wall-clock time versus a single agent doing it alone.

quiz: When does multi-agent beat a single agent, and when is it a waste of tokens?
How does the orchestrator stop workers from duplicating work?

modules.title: Capstone: a mini Wafer
modules.goal: The agent from this track drives the Inference Systems capstone. One project, two tracks.

blocks.label: Deliverables (shared with Inference Systems week 7)
items: Reuse your Week 3 MCP tools for benchmarking.
Use your Week 5 evals to check the agent picks a correct, faster config at least 4 of 5 times.
Record a 2-minute demo video of the agent searching and picking a winner.
Write the project up as one resume bullet with a real speedup number.

quiz: Where did your agent fail during the capstone, and what did you change?
